title: What I Built Instead
author: mrsk04
summary: A mother recounts building a custom reading curriculum for her dyslexic daughter after the public school system repeatedly failed to identify, acknowledge, or remediate her reading difficulties. The piece documents the multi-year journey from early concerns (age 5) to formal dyslexia diagnosis (age 8) to the mother's decision to construct her own Orton-Gillingham-based intervention program when the school's reading specialist offered nothing systematic. She teaches herself the science of reading, purchases structured literacy materials, and runs daily intervention sessions before school. The daughter makes two years of reading progress in eight months. The piece is both a personal narrative and a quiet indictment of how schools handle dyslexia: they wait, they normalize the struggle, and they rarely tell parents that evidence-based tools exist. The mother's closing argument is that no parent should have to become a reading specialist to get their child what research has known how to provide for decades.
points: * The school system failed to identify dyslexia until age 8 despite the mother raising concerns repeatedly from age 5 -- a pattern consistent with research showing schools routinely delay diagnosis to avoid service obligations. * Once the diagnosis was confirmed, the school's reading specialist offered no systematic intervention; the mother had to learn Orton-Gillingham principles independently and purchase structured literacy materials herself. * The mother's home intervention produced two years of reading progress in eight months using structured literacy -- a result consistent with peer-reviewed research on Orton-Gillingham effectiveness that the school system had access to but did not use. * The piece documents a specific structural failure: schools rarely communicate to parents that evidence-based dyslexia interventions exist, leaving families who cannot afford private tutors without a path forward. * The closing argument is systemic: the problem is not individual teacher negligence but institutional inertia -- schools know the science, they have known it for decades, and they have not deployed it.
quotes: I spent three years being told she would 'catch up,' that she was 'just a little behind,' that 'some kids develop later.' I spent three years watching her cry over books while her classmates moved on.

When the diagnosis finally came at age eight, I expected the school to tell me what to do next. Instead, the reading specialist handed me a packet of worksheets and told me to 'practice reading at home.' That was it. That was the plan.

I bought the Barton Reading and Spelling System. I read everything I could find about Orton-Gillingham. I ran 30-minute sessions before school every morning. My daughter went from reading at a kindergarten level to a second-grade level in eight months.

The science of reading has been settled for decades. The research on dyslexia is not controversial. Every school in the country has access to the same evidence I found on my laptop in my kitchen. They have just chosen not to act on it.

No parent should have to become a reading specialist to get their child what research has known how to provide for thirty years. The fact that I had to is not a personal achievement. It is a systemic indictment.
